summary: Describes the Access Node Control Protocol, which runs between a Network Access Server and an access node such as a DSLAM in a broadband network. It supports operations related to quality of service, services, and subscribers, and includes capabilities beyond the base protocol.

plainLanguage.summary:
A broadband network has two kinds of box. At the end of the customer's line is an access node, which turns the line into network traffic. Further in is the network access server, which gathers the traffic from many lines and applies policy to it. They often need to exchange information: which line is which, what service profile a line should have, and whether a line is working.

ANCP is the protocol for that conversation. The two ends first shake hands to confirm they are in step, then exchange messages built from typed blocks of data. The first version covers digital subscriber lines, and the design leaves room for other kinds of access network to be added later.

questions: how does a nas control a dslam
what is the ancp adjacency protocol
how does a nas configure a dslam line
subtitle: A control protocol between the equipment that ends a broadband line and the network that bills for it.

tldr.problem: The equipment in the street that terminates a subscriber's line and the network edge device that aggregates many of those lines need to agree about quality of service, service profiles and subscribers. Without a protocol between them, the information is either duplicated by hand or missing.
tldr.mechanism: ANCP defines a message format, an adjacency handshake to keep the two sides in step, and a set of capabilities, starting with DSL topology discovery, line configuration and remote line testing. The messages travel over TCP inside IPsec.
tldr.outcome: The access network and its aggregation point can exchange line state, configure services and run tests over one protocol that can be extended for other access technologies. RFC 7256 later updated this document.

facts.label: Transport
facts.value: TCP inside IPsec, with IKEv2 for key management

facts.label: ANCP version number
facts.value: 50, in the joint GSMP and ANCP registry

today: RFC 6320 is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted, and it was updated by RFC 7256, which adds multicast control extensions for the Access Node Control Protocol.

sections.title: What ANCP Connects
sections.content:
The document defines the Access Node Control Protocol, which realizes a control plane between a service-oriented layer 3 edge device, the Network Access Server, and a layer 2 Access Node such as a Digital Subscriber Line Access Multiplexer, in order to perform operations related to quality of service, services and subscriptions. The requirements for ANCP and the context within which it operates are described in RFC 5851.

ANCP provides its services to control applications operating in the Access Node and in the Network Access Server. Each side runs an ANCP agent, and the two agents exchange ANCP messages. Specification of the control applications is beyond the scope of the document, but informative partial descriptions are given as necessary to give context for the operation of the protocol. The document specifies ANCP transport over TCP and IP.

The organization of the document is: Section 2 describes the access networks within which ANCP will typically be deployed; Section 3 specifies generally applicable aspects of ANCP; Section 4 specifies messages and TLVs intended for use by multiple capabilities spanning multiple technologies; Sections 5 to 8 specify the ANCP implementation of three capabilities applicable to the control of DSL access technology, namely topology discovery, line configuration and remote line connectivity testing; Section 9 covers the IANA registries, including the joint GSMP and ANCP version registry; and Section 11 addresses security considerations.

Historical note. Initial implementations of the protocol that became ANCP were based on the General Switch Management Protocol version 3. The ANCP charter required the Working Group to develop its protocol based on these implementations. In the end ANCP introduced so many extensions and modifications that the two protocols are not interoperable. Nevertheless, although this specification has no normative dependencies on GSMPv3, the mark of ANCP's origins can be seen in the various unused fields within the ANCP message header. Early in ANCP's development the decision was made to use the same TCP port and encapsulation as GSMPv3, and by the time ANCP was finished it was too late to reverse that decision because of existing implementations. As a result there must be a way for an ANCP peer to quickly distinguish ANCP from GSMP during initial adjacency negotiations, and this has been provided by a joint registry of GSMP and ANCP version numbers. GSMP has version numbers 1 through 3; ANCP has the initial version number 50.
sections.plainLanguage: ANCP fills a gap between two pieces of equipment that both need to know about the subscriber lines. It grew out of an older protocol, GSMP, but changed so much that the two cannot talk to each other, so it needed its own version number.

sections.title: The Pieces of the System
sections.content:
The terminology repeats some definitions from RFC 5851 and adds terms used only in this document.

The Access Node is a network device, usually located at a service provider central office or street cabinet, that terminates access loop connections from subscribers. In the case of a Digital Subscriber Line, the Access Node provides DSL signal termination and is referred to as a DSL Access Multiplexer. The Network Access Server is a network element that aggregates subscriber traffic from a number of Access Nodes; it is an enforcement point for policy management and IP quality of service in the access network, and is also referred to as a Broadband Network Gateway or Broadband Remote Access Server. The Home Gateway is the network element that connects subscriber devices to the Access Node and the access network; in the case of DSL it is a DSL network termination that may operate either as a layer 2 bridge or as a layer 3 router, in which case it is also called a Routing Gateway.

An ANCP agent is a logical entity that implements ANCP in the Access Node, on the AN side, or in the NAS, on the NAS side. The Access Node control adjacency is the relationship between the two ANCP agents for the purpose of exchanging ANCP messages; the adjacency may be either up or down, depending on the result of the adjacency protocol operation. An ANCP capability is a specific set of ANCP messages, message content and procedures required to implement a specific use case or set of use cases; some capabilities apply to one access technology while others are technology independent, and the capabilities applicable to a given adjacency are negotiated during adjacency startup.

A Type-Length-Value structure consists of a 16-bit type field, a 16-bit length field and a variable-length value field padded to the nearest 32-bit word boundary. The value field can contain other TLVs, and an IANA registry is maintained for the values of the type field.

Net data rate is the portion of the total data rate that can be used to transmit user information, such as ATM cells or Ethernet frames; it excludes overhead that pertains to the physical transmission mechanism, such as trellis coding in the case of DSL, and includes TPS-TC encapsulation, which is zero for ATM encapsulation and non-zero for 64/65 encapsulation. Line rate contains the complete overhead including Reed-Solomon and trellis coding. DSL multi-pair bonding is a method for bonding multiple xDSL access lines into a single bidirectional logical link, allowing an operator to combine the data rates on two or more copper pairs and deliver the aggregate data rate to a single customer.
sections.plainLanguage: The document names each part precisely, because the messages travel between boxes with very different jobs: the box at the end of the line, the box that gathers many lines, and the customer's own equipment in between.

sections.title: Transport and Framing
sections.content:
The document specifies the use of TCP with IPsec and IKEv2 over IP for transport of ANCP messages, and other specifications may introduce additional transports in the future. In the case of ATM access, a separate permanent virtual circuit that acts as a control channel and is capable of transporting IP MAY be configured between the NAS and the AN. In the case of an Ethernet access and aggregation network, a typical practice is to send the ANCP messages over a dedicated Ethernet virtual LAN using a separate VLAN identifier.

When transported over TCP, ANCP messages MUST use an encapsulation consisting of a 4-byte header field prepended to the ANCP message. The Identifier field is 16 bits and identifies a GSMP or ANCP message; it MUST be set to 0x880C. The Length field is 16 bits and gives the total length of the ANCP message in bytes, not including the 4-byte encapsulating header.

The Access Node MUST initiate the TCP session to the NAS, using destination port 6068. This is necessary to avoid static address provisioning on the NAS for all the Access Nodes it serves, since it is easier to configure a given Access Node with the single IP address of the NAS that serves it. The NAS MUST listen on port 6068 for incoming connections from the Access Nodes. In the event of an ANCP transport protocol failure, all pending ANCP messages destined for the disconnected recipient SHOULD be discarded until the transport connection is re-established.

All text fields in ANCP use UTF-8 encoding. When extracting text fields from a message, the ANCP agent MUST NOT assume that the fields are zero-terminated. ANCP messages contain a number of fields that are unused or reserved: some are always unused, typically because they were inherited from GSMPv3, and others are reserved for future extensions. Both reserved and unused fields MUST be set to zeroes by the sender and MUST be ignored by the receiver.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message is preceded by a four-byte header that says which protocol it is and how long it is. The box at the end of the line always dials the network edge, so the network edge does not need a configured address for every line it serves.

sections.title: The Adjacency Protocol
sections.content:
ANCP uses the adjacency protocol to synchronize the NAS and the Access Nodes and to maintain the ANCP session. After the TCP connection is established, adjacency protocol messages MUST be exchanged. ANCP messages other than adjacency protocol messages MUST NOT be sent until the adjacency protocol has achieved synchronization.

The adjacency protocol operates symmetrically between the NAS and the AN. In the absence of errors or race conditions, each peer sends a SYN message, receives a SYNACK message in acknowledgement, and completes the establishment of the adjacency by sending an ACK message. Through this exchange each peer learns the Name, Port and Instance parameters identifying the other peer, and the two peers negotiate the values of the Version, Timer, P Flag and Partition ID parameters and the set of capabilities that the adjacency will support.

Once the adjacency has been established, its liveness is periodically tested, with the peers exchanging ACK messages at a frequency determined by the negotiated value of the Timer field. If an inconsistency, loss of contact or protocol violation is detected, the detecting peer can force a restart of the synchronization process by sending an RSTACK message to the other end. Once an adjacency has been established, if more than one NAS has established an adjacency to the same partition, the AN sends an Adjacency Update message to each such NAS to let it know how many established adjacencies the partition currently supports; similarly, if an adjacency is lost, the AN sends an Adjacency Update message to each of the remaining adjacent NASs.

The protocol has three states, SYNSENT, SYNRCVD and ESTAB, plus the reset operation. The reset procedure generates a new instance number for the link, deletes the peer verifier by setting the stored Sender Instance, Sender Port and Sender Name to zero, sends a SYN message and enters the SYNSENT state. A timer is required for the periodic generation of SYN, SYNACK and ACK messages; the value is negotiated in the Timer field, the period is unspecified, and a value of 25 seconds is suggested. Since ANCP uses a reliable transport protocol, the timer is unlikely to expire in any state other than ESTAB.

When the timer expires, the rules are: in SYNSENT send SYN, in SYNRCVD send SYNACK, in ESTAB send ACK. When a packet arrives and it is an RSTACK, the link is reset if the conditions hold and the peer is not in SYNSENT; otherwise the message is discarded. When a packet arrives and it is a SYN, SYNACK or ACK, the state tables apply. When a packet arrives and it is any other ANCP message and the state is not ESTAB, the incoming message is discarded and a SYN or SYNACK is sent as appropriate, with no more than two SYN or SYNACK messages sent within any period of length defined by the timer.

State synchronization across a link is considered to be achieved when the protocol reaches the ESTAB state. All ANCP messages other than adjacency protocol messages that are received before synchronization is achieved will be discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: Before anything else can be said, the two ends confirm they are talking to each other and agree on what they can do. If one of them sees something inconsistent, it can tell the other to start over. A regular exchange of acknowledgements then proves the link is still alive.

sections.title: The Message Header and the TLVs
sections.content:
All ANCP messages other than adjacency messages share a common header format. The Version field of 8 bits carries the version of ANCP agreed during adjacency negotiation. The Message Type field of 8 bits indicates the ANCP message type, and message type values are registered in an IANA registry. The Result field of 4 bits indicates, in request messages, the circumstances under which a response is required, and in responses indicates either Success or Failure. The Result Code field of 12 bits gives further information about the result, mostly an error code in a failure response; in a request message it is not used and MUST be set to zero.

The five Result values are Ignore (0x0), where the field is treated as a no operation and the response procedures for the received message type are followed; Nack (0x1), where a response is expected only in cases of failure during processing; AckAll (0x2), where a response is requested in all cases; Success (0x3), where the request was executed successfully; and Failure (0x4), where the request was not executed successfully and the receiver should take further action as indicated by the Result Code and any diagnostic data in a Status-Info TLV.

The remaining header fields are the Partition ID of 8 bits, the Transaction Identifier of 24 bits, which distinguishes between multiple request messages of the same type and associates a response with a request, the I Flag and SubMessage Number of 1 plus 15 bits, and the Length of 16 bits. The Transaction ID is used to distinguish between multiple request messages of the same type and to associate a response message to a request, and the specification for a response message should indicate in all cases that the value of the Transaction Identifier MUST be set to that of the corresponding request message.

The message payload consists of zero or more fixed fields followed by a variable amount of data in the form of Type-Length-Value structures. A TLV has a 16-bit Type field identifying the type and nature of its contents, with an IANA registry established for the codes, a 16-bit Length field giving the number of bytes in the Value field excluding any padding needed to bring the TLV to a 4-byte word boundary, and a variable Value field that MUST be padded with zeroes to align with a 4-byte word boundary. The Value field of a TLV MAY include fixed fields and other TLVs. Unless otherwise specified, TLVs MAY be added to a message in any order, and if the recipient of a message does not understand a particular TLV it MUST silently ignore it.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message starts with the same twelve-byte header: which protocol version, which kind of message, whether it worked, which transaction it belongs to and how long the body is. The body is a list of typed blocks, each with a type number, a length and the data. A receiver that does not recognise a block skips it and reads the rest.

sections.title: The Three DSL Capabilities
sections.content:
DSL is a widely deployed access technology for broadband access networks, and specifications describe possible architectures for these access networks, covering the delivery of voice, video and data services. The next three sections of the document specify basic ANCP capabilities for use specifically in controlling Access Nodes serving DSL access, where the technology type is 0x05. The same Access Nodes could be serving other access technologies such as Metro-Ethernet, Passive Optical Networking and WiMax, in which case the AN will also have to support the corresponding other-technology-specific capabilities, which are outside the scope of this document.

Access line identification. Most ANCP messages involve actions relating to a specific access line, so a way of describing access lines within those messages is needed. Four TLVs are defined for that purpose, covering identification of an access line by its logical appearance on the user side of the Access Node, by its remote identification, and by binary or ASCII identifiers of the access aggregation circuit.

DSL topology discovery. The Access Node reports the state of its ports, and the NAS uses that information to keep its own picture of the access network up to date. The procedures define what the AN side and the NAS side do, and Port Up and Port Down event messages report changes. A set of TLVs describes the line attributes, including the DSL type, the actual, minimum, attainable and maximum net data rates in each direction, minimum net low-power data rates, maximum and actual interleaving delays, the DSL line state and the access loop encapsulation.

DSL line configuration. The NAS can ask the Access Node to put a subscriber line into a particular service profile. The Port Management message for line configuration carries access line identifying TLVs and line configuration TLVs, and its Message Type field MUST be set to 32. The Result field MUST be set to either Nack or AckAll as determined by policy on the NAS, and the 24-bit Transaction Identifier field MUST be set to a positive value.

DSL remote line connectivity testing. The Port Management message for line testing has the same format as for line configuration, with three differences: the Result field in the request SHOULD be set to AckAll, to allow the NAS to receive the information contained in a successful test response; the Function field MUST be set to 9, meaning Remote Loopback, with the X-Function field continuing to be 0; and the appended TLVs in the extension value field include testing-related TLVs rather than subscriber service information. The testing TLVs are the OAM Loopback Test Parameters TLV, the Opaque Data TLV and the OAM Loopback Test Response String TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: Three jobs are defined for DSL lines: working out which line is which and how fast it currently is, putting a subscriber onto a service profile, and running a loopback test to check the line works. Each is a set of message types and typed data blocks that a future extension could copy for other kinds of access network.

sections.title: The Registries
sections.content:
The document defines a number of new ANCP-specific registries as well as the joint GSMP and ANCP version registry.

The ANCP Message Types registry holds values that may range from 0 to 255, with new message types SHOULD being assigned sequentially from 90 onwards, noting that 91 and 93 are already assigned. The initial contents are message type 10 for the Adjacency Protocol, 32 for Port Management, 80 for Port Up, 81 for Port Down, 85 for Adjacency Update, 91 for Generic Response and 93 for Provisioning.

The other registries are the ANCP Result Code registry, the ANCP Port Management Function registry, the ANCP Technology Type registry, the ANCP Command Code registry, the ANCP TLV Type registry and the ANCP Capability Type registry. Additions to these registries are permitted by Standards Action.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message type, result code and typed block gets a number from IANA, so that different vendors agree on what the numbers mean and can extend the protocol without colliding.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security of ANCP is discussed in RFC 5713, and a number of security requirements are stated in Section 8 of that document. The protocol solution MUST offer authentication of the AN to the NAS and authentication of the NAS to the AN. It MUST allow authorization to take place at the NAS and the AN, MUST offer replay protection, MUST provide data-origin authentication, and MUST be robust against denial-of-service attacks. It SHOULD offer confidentiality protection, and SHOULD ensure that operations in default configuration guarantee a low number of AN and NAS protocol interactions.

For secure transport, either the combination of IPsec with IKEv2 or the use of TLS will meet the requirements listed above. However, the use of TLS has been rejected. The deciding point is a detail of protocol design that was unavailable when RFC 5713 was written: the ANCP adjacency is a major point of vulnerability for denial-of-service attacks. If the adjacency can be shut down, either the AN clears its state pending reestablishment of the adjacency, or the possibility of mismatches between the AN's and NAS's view of state on the AN is opened up. Two ways to cause an adjacency to be taken down are to modify messages so that the ANCP agents conclude that they are no longer synchronized, or to attack the underlying TCP session. TLS will protect message contents but not the TCP connection, and one has to use either IPsec or the TCP authentication option for that. Hence ANCP MUST run over IPsec with IKEv2 for authentication and key management.

In greater detail, the ANCP stack MUST include IPsec running in transport mode, since the AN and NAS are the endpoints of the path. The Encapsulating Security Payload MUST be used in order to satisfy the requirement for data confidentiality, and MUST be configured for the combination of confidentiality, integrity and anti-replay capability. The traffic flow confidentiality service of ESP is unnecessary and, in fact, unworkable in the case of ANCP. IKEv2 is also REQUIRED, to meet the requirements for mutual authentication and authorization. Since the NAS and AN MAY be in different trust domains, the use of certificates for mutual authentication could be the most practical approach, although this is up to the operators concerned. The AN MUST play the role of initiator of the IKEv2 conversation.
sections.plainLanguage: ANCP must run inside IPsec, with IKEv2 setting up the keys. The reason TLS was rejected is specific: an attacker who can break the TCP session can make the two sides disagree about their state, and TLS does not protect the TCP session itself.

messages.label: SYN
messages.note: Sends the AN's name, port and instance, and the capabilities it offers.

messages.label: SYNACK
messages.note: Acknowledges the SYN and answers with the NAS's own parameters.

messages.label: ACK
messages.note: Completes the handshake. The adjacency is now ESTAB and other messages may flow.

fields.name: Identifier
fields.desc: Identifies a GSMP or ANCP message. It MUST be set to 0x880C.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Total length of the ANCP message in bytes, not counting this header.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: The version of ANCP agreed during adjacency negotiation.

fields.name: Message Type
fields.desc: The ANCP message type. Values are registered in an IANA registry.

fields.name: Result
fields.desc: In a request, when a response is wanted. In a response, Success (0x3) or Failure (0x4).

fields.name: Result Code
fields.desc: Further detail on the result, usually an error code. Set to zero in a request.

fields.name: Partition ID
fields.desc: Identifies the partition the adjacency belongs to.

fields.name: Transaction Identifier
fields.desc: Ties a response to its request and distinguishes requests of the same type.

fields.name: I Flag and SubMessage Number
fields.desc: One flag bit and a 15-bit submessage number.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the message payload that follows the header.

items.label: Ignore
items.desc: Treat the field as a no operation and follow the response procedures for the message type.

items.label: Nack
items.desc: Respond only if processing the message contents fails.

items.label: AckAll
items.desc: A response is requested in all cases.

items.label: Success
items.desc: This is a response and the request was executed successfully.

items.label: Failure
items.desc: This is a response and the request was not executed successfully.

items.label: Adjacency Protocol
items.desc: The SYN, SYNACK, ACK and RSTACK messages of the adjacency handshake.

items.label: Port Management
items.desc: Used for DSL line configuration and for remote line connectivity testing.

items.label: Port Up
items.desc: Reports that a port has come up.

items.label: Port Down
items.desc: Reports that a port has gone down.

items.label: Adjacency Update
items.desc: Reports a change in the number of established adjacencies for a partition.

items.label: Generic Response
items.desc: A response that is not tied to one message type.

items.label: Provisioning
items.desc: Provisions information of global scope on the Access Node.

items.title: Topology discovery
items.text: The Access Node reports its port state and line attributes so the NAS can keep its picture of the access network current.

items.title: Line configuration
items.text: The NAS asks the Access Node to put a subscriber line into a named service profile.

items.title: Remote line testing
items.text: A Port Management message with the Remote Loopback function runs a test on the line and returns the result.
